title: Tool-Using Agent From Scratch
tagline: Build a working reason-act-observe agent loop in raw Python with no framework, so you understand every moving part before you ever import one.
summary: You'll build a tool-using LLM agent from first principles in plain Python, with no agent framework of any kind. Starting from a single model call, you'll define a small catalog of tools with typed schemas, teach the model how to request a tool, parse those requests out of the model's output, execute the tool, and feed the observation back into the conversation so the model can reason again. You'll wrap it all in a bounded reason-act-observe loop with a hard step cap so it can never run forever, and hide the provider behind a thin client wrapper so the same agent works whether you point it at one API or another. This is the mental model the entire ladder builds on: by the end you'll know exactly what LangGraph, MCP, and multi-agent systems are doing under the hood, because you'll have written the primitive version yourself. Everything runs locally against your own model API key.
scenario: You've been asked to prototype an internal assistant that can actually do things, not just chat: look up the current time, do arithmetic reliably, and read a small local knowledge file to answer questions. Your team is framework-shy after getting burned by a heavy dependency that broke on an upgrade, so the mandate is deliberately minimal: build the smallest honest agent that works, in code you fully understand, that a teammate could read top to bottom in one sitting. You reach for nothing but the standard library and a single model SDK. The goal isn't a product, it's fluency: when the agent misbehaves you must be able to point at the exact line where reasoning became action, and fix it.
learningGoals: Explain the reason-act-observe agent loop and why observations must be fed back into the model's context
Design a tool as a Python function plus a machine-readable schema the model can be shown
Prompt a model to emit a structured tool call and parse that call reliably out of its response
Execute a requested tool safely and format the result as an observation the model can consume
Bound an agent with a step cap and stop conditions so it always terminates
Abstract the model provider behind a thin, swappable client wrapper for portability
skillsDemonstrated: Implemented an LLM agent loop from scratch in pure Python without any agent framework
Designed a tool interface with JSON-serializable schemas and a dispatch registry
Parsed and validated model-generated tool calls, handling malformed output gracefully
Built a bounded control loop with a step cap, final-answer detection, and error recovery
Wrote a provider-agnostic model client wrapper to decouple agent logic from any single API
Structured a small, readable Python project with configuration via environment variables
techStack: A model provider SDK (Anthropic, OpenAI, or any chat-completions API)
Standard library json, re, dataclasses, typing
Rich or plain logging (readable trace output)
prerequisites: Comfortable writing Python functions, dictionaries, and simple classes
Basic understanding of what an LLM chat completion is (messages in, text out)
A model provider API key you can set as an environment variable
Familiarity with the command line and running Python scripts
Able to read and write JSON structures in Python
datasetDescription: Domain model & sample data / corpus: There is no external dataset. The 'corpus' is a small local notes.md file (a few short facts about a fictional company, e.g. office locations, support hours, a product list) that one of the tools reads so the agent has something grounded to look things up in. The tool catalog itself is the domain model: get_current_time() returning an ISO timestamp, calculator(expression) evaluating a safe arithmetic expression, and read_notes(query) doing a naive substring search over notes.md. Each tool is described by a schema dict with a name, a one-line description, and a parameters object listing argument names, types, and whether they're required. Sample conversations (multi-step questions like 'what is 12.5% of our 240 support tickets, and when do support hours end today?') are kept in a fixtures file to drive tests.
architectureFlow: User question -> Build message list (system prompt + tool schemas + history) -> Model client wrapper (provider-agnostic call) -> Model response text -> Parse for a tool call -> [tool call found: dispatch to tool registry -> execute tool -> format observation -> append to messages -> loop again (step counter++)] or [final answer found: return to user] -> Step cap reached? -> stop with best-effort answer

milestones.title: Project Setup & a Single Model Call

hints: For safe arithmetic, parse with the ast module and allow only numeric/operator nodes rather than calling eval()

Write test_parser.py covering a valid tool call, a final answer, malformed JSON, and an unknown tool name

hints: Ask the model to emit exactly one JSON object per turn; a fenced code block is easy to locate with a regex

milestones.title: Close the Loop: Execute, Observe, Reason Again
milestones.goal: Wire tool execution and observation feedback into a working reason-act-observe cycle that keeps going until the model gives a final answer.
tasks: In agent.py, write a run(question) that seeds messages with the system prompt and the user question

milestones.title: Bound It: Step Cap, Stop Conditions & Safety

acceptanceCriteria: The loop always terminates within MAX_STEPS and reports when the cap was reached

hints: Inject the llm_client as a dependency so tests can pass a stub that returns scripted responses

milestones.deliverable: A bounded, crash-resistant agent with a step cap, loop detection, and a deterministic offline test suite.

title: RAG Assistant Over Your Docs
tagline: Build a retrieval-augmented assistant that answers questions from your own documents with citations, and prove it works with a real eval set.
summary: You'll build a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) assistant that answers questions grounded in a document collection you provide, and cites where each answer came from. You'll implement the full pipeline yourself: ingest raw documents, chunk them thoughtfully, embed the chunks, store them in a vector index, retrieve the top-k most relevant chunks for a question, and prompt the model to answer using only that retrieved context, with inline citations back to the source. Crucially, you won't stop at 'it seems to work': you'll build a small evaluation set and measure the system with recall@k for retrieval quality and a faithfulness check for whether answers stay grounded in the retrieved text. This turns RAG from a demo into something you can iterate on with numbers. Everything runs locally against your own model and embedding API keys, with a local vector store so there's zero external infrastructure to manage.
scenario: Your team drowns in internal documentation, onboarding guides, runbooks, and policy docs, and people keep asking questions that are answered somewhere in those files but nobody can find fast. You're asked to build an assistant that answers those questions directly from the docs and, critically, cites the source so answers are trustworthy and auditable. Leadership has been burned by a flashy demo that confidently made things up, so the requirement is explicit: the assistant must ground every answer in retrieved content, refuse to answer when the docs don't cover it, and come with evidence that it retrieves the right material and doesn't hallucinate. Your job is to build that pipeline and back it with a small but honest evaluation.
learningGoals: Design a document ingestion and chunking strategy that balances context size against retrieval precision
Generate embeddings and store them in a vector index for similarity search
Implement top-k retrieval and assemble a grounded prompt from retrieved chunks
Prompt a model to answer only from provided context and produce inline source citations
Make the assistant abstain when the retrieved context does not contain the answer
Evaluate a RAG system with retrieval metrics (recall@k) and a faithfulness/groundedness check
skillsDemonstrated: Built an end-to-end RAG pipeline: ingest, chunk, embed, index, retrieve, and generate
Implemented semantic retrieval over a local vector store with top-k similarity search
Engineered grounded, citation-bearing prompts that constrain the model to retrieved context
Designed abstention behavior so the assistant declines when evidence is missing
Constructed a labeled evaluation set and measured recall@k and answer faithfulness
Ran retrieval experiments (chunk size, k) and used metrics to justify configuration choices
techStack: An embeddings API or a local sentence-transformers model
A vector store (Chroma, FAISS, or LanceDB, all local)
prerequisites: Completion of Project 1 (Tool-Using Agent) or equivalent comfort with LLM calls in Python
Comfortable with Python: functions, classes, file I/O, list/dict manipulation
Basic understanding of what an embedding vector represents
A model API key and an embeddings source (API key or local model) set via environment variables
Familiarity with running scripts and pytest from the command line
datasetDescription: Domain model & sample data / corpus: You supply a small corpus of 15-40 documents, a mix of Markdown and PDF, representing an internal knowledge base (onboarding notes, a few runbooks, an HR policy, a product FAQ). Fictional or public-domain content is fine as long as it's varied enough that retrieval matters. The pipeline treats each document as a source with an id, title, and path; after chunking, each chunk carries chunk_id, source_id, the text, and a position offset used for citations. A companion eval file (eval/questions.jsonl) holds 15-25 hand-written questions, each labeled with the id(s) of the chunk or document that actually contains the answer (the gold set for recall@k) and a short reference answer used for the faithfulness check. A few adversarial questions whose answers are NOT in the corpus are included to test abstention.
architectureFlow: Raw documents (md/pdf) -> Ingest (parse to text + metadata) -> Chunk (size/overlap strategy) -> Embed (embedding model) -> Vector index (local store) -> [query time] User question -> Embed query -> Top-k similarity search -> Assemble grounded prompt (chunks + citations) -> Model generation -> Answer with inline citations OR abstain -> Eval harness (recall@k over gold chunks + faithfulness check)

milestones.title: Ingest & Chunk the Corpus

title: LangGraph Agent with State, Checkpoints & Human-in-the-Loop
tagline: Rebuild your agent as a durable state graph that persists progress, streams its thinking, and pauses for human approval before doing anything risky.
summary: Now that you've built an agent by hand, you'll rebuild it properly as an explicit state machine using LangGraph. Instead of an ad-hoc loop, you'll model the agent as a graph of nodes and edges over a typed shared state, which makes control flow inspectable and testable. You'll wire in a checkpointer so the agent's state persists between steps and across process restarts, meaning a run can be resumed exactly where it left off. You'll stream the graph's events so you can watch reasoning and tool calls unfold in real time. And you'll implement the capability that matters most in production: a human-in-the-loop approval interrupt that pauses the graph before a risky tool (like sending an email or deleting a record) and only proceeds once a human approves, with the whole thing surviving a restart while it waits. Everything runs locally against your own model API key with a local checkpoint store.
scenario: Your from-scratch agent works, but the team won't let it touch anything consequential: it can't send messages, modify records, or spend money without a person signing off, and if the process dies mid-task everyone has to start over. The mandate is to make the agent durable and governable. It must persist its state so a long-running task survives a crash or a deploy and resumes cleanly. Operators need to watch what it's doing as it happens, not read logs after the fact. And any action with real-world consequences must stop and wait for explicit human approval, potentially minutes or hours later, without losing its place. You choose LangGraph because it gives you first-class state, checkpointing, streaming, and interrupts, exactly the production primitives your hand-rolled loop was missing.

title: MCP Server + Client Agent
tagline: Build a Model Context Protocol server that safely exposes tools and resources, then a client agent that discovers and calls them over the wire.
summary: You'll learn the interoperability standard that lets agents and tools talk to each other: the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Instead of hardcoding tools into an agent, you'll build a standalone MCP server that exposes a small set of well-scoped, safe tools and resources, describing them with proper schemas so any MCP-aware client can understand and use them. Then you'll build a client agent that connects to the server, discovers the available tools and resources at runtime, and calls them as part of its reasoning loop, without knowing anything about them ahead of time. This decoupling is the whole point: tools live behind a standard protocol boundary, and agents consume them dynamically. You'll handle the transport, the capability handshake, input validation, and safe error responses across the boundary. Everything runs locally, with the agent's model calls using your own API key and the MCP server running as a separate local process.
scenario: Your organization is accumulating internal capabilities, a document store, a ticketing system, a metrics API, and every team is tempted to bolt them directly into their own agent. That path leads to N agents each with their own brittle, duplicated integrations. The architecture lead mandates a cleaner pattern: expose capabilities behind the Model Context Protocol so they're described once, in one place, with clear schemas and safety boundaries, and let any agent discover and use them dynamically. You're tasked with proving the pattern end to end: build a small MCP server exposing two or three safe capabilities, and a client agent that connects, discovers what's available, and uses those capabilities to answer questions, demonstrating that tools and agents can now evolve independently.

datasetDescription: Domain model & sample data / corpus: No external dataset. The MCP server exposes a small, safe capability surface backed by tiny local fixtures. Tools: search_docs(query) does a substring search over a handful of local Markdown files, and get_weather(city) returns a canned/mock forecast for a fixed set of cities (deterministic, no external call). Resource: a read-only 'company://handbook' resource that serves the text of a local handbook.md so the client can fetch reference content. Each tool declares a name, description, and a pydantic-validated input schema; the resource declares a URI and mime type. title: Multi-Agent Supervisor System
tagline: Build a supervisor agent that routes subtasks to specialist workers, coordinates their handoffs over shared state, and synthesizes their results.
summary: You'll graduate from a single agent to a coordinated team. In this project a supervisor agent decomposes a user's request, routes each subtask to the right specialist worker agent (for example a researcher, a coder/analyst, and a writer), and orchestrates the handoffs between them over a shared state. Each worker is focused and good at one thing; the supervisor decides who works next, passes along the accumulated context, and knows when the task is done. You'll design the shared-state contract that flows between agents, implement the routing logic that turns the supervisor into a controller rather than a doer, handle handoffs so context isn't lost, and finally have the supervisor synthesize the workers' outputs into a single coherent answer. You'll also confront the real hazards of multi-agent systems: infinite ping-pong between agents, runaway cost, and lost context. Everything runs locally against your own model API key, and you can build it on LangGraph (recommended, reusing Project 3) or extend your from-scratch loop.
scenario: Your single-agent assistant is now being asked to handle requests that are genuinely multi-disciplinary: 'research this topic, analyze the numbers, and write me a brief.' Cramming all of that into one prompt produces a mediocre generalist that does each part poorly and blows the context window. The team wants a system that mirrors how a real team works: a coordinator who understands the whole request and delegates to specialists, each with a tight, focused role, and who then assembles their work into a polished deliverable. You're asked to build a supervisor-and-workers architecture, prove it routes intelligently, keeps context flowing across handoffs, and terminates reliably, and to do it without the agents endlessly bouncing work back and forth or running up an unbounded bill.

title: Production Agent Capstone
tagline: Take an agent all the way to production: an eval harness, tracing, guardrails, injection defense, cost/latency controls, and a real deploy story.
summary: This capstone ties the whole domain together by taking one of your earlier agents (or a fresh one built on those skills) and hardening it into something you could actually operate. You'll build an evaluation harness that combines an LLM-as-judge with a regression suite so you can prove the agent got better, not worse, on every change. You'll add tracing and observability so every run is inspectable, with spans for reasoning, tool calls, latency, and token usage. You'll implement guardrails: input validation, output validation, and defenses against prompt injection and tool misuse. You'll put in cost and latency controls, budgets, timeouts, caching, and model routing, so the agent is affordable and responsive. And you'll write a real deploy story: containerize the agent, expose it behind an API, add health checks and structured logging, and document how to run and monitor it. This is the difference between an impressive demo and a system a team would trust in production. Everything runs locally with the learner's own model API key, and the deploy story is reproducible on any machine.
scenario: One of your agents is good enough that stakeholders want to put it in front of real users, and now every hard production question lands at once. How do you know a prompt tweak didn't silently regress quality? What happens when a user pastes hostile text trying to hijack the agent or trick it into calling a dangerous tool? Who's paying the bill when a single query fans out into twenty model calls? When it misbehaves at 2am, how does anyone debug it? Leadership won't ship without answers. Your job for the capstone is to close every one of those gaps: measurable quality with an eval harness and regression tests, defense against injection and misuse, cost and latency under control, full observability into every run, and a documented, reproducible deploy. You take the agent from 'cool demo' to 'we can operate this.'

Lead the README with the architecture diagram and the scorecard; together they tell the whole production story
milestones.deliverable: A containerized, API-served, observable agent with health checks, structured logs, and a documented deploy and eval scorecard.

productionChecklist: Quality is measured by an eval harness (LLM-as-judge + regression) and a regression suite guards critical behavior
Every run is traced with per-run latency, token, and cost accounting
Input guardrails detect and neutralize prompt injection and reject malicious requests
Tool use is constrained by an allowlist and argument validation to prevent misuse
Output is validated for shape and safety before it is returned
Per-run budgets and timeouts bound cost and latency, with caching and model routing to reduce both
The agent is served behind an API with a health check and structured JSON logging
It is containerized and reproducible, uses the learner's own API key from the environment, and secrets are never committed
stretchGoals: Add a canary/A-B path so a new prompt or model runs on a fraction of traffic and is compared on the scorecard
Add rate limiting and per-user cost budgets to the API
Add automated alerting when the eval scorecard, error rate, or cost per request crosses a threshold
Add red-teaming: generate new adversarial cases automatically and fold failures back into the eval set
Deploy to a real host (a small cloud service) and document the production URL and monitoring dashboard
portfolioTips: This capstone is the crown of your agent portfolio because it answers the questions every hiring manager actually asks: how do you know it works, how do you keep it safe, and how do you run it. Lead with the eval scorecard (broken out by happy-path, edge-case, and adversarial) and a short writeup of a prompt-injection attack your guardrails defeated, since measurable quality and demonstrated safety are the rarest signals in agent portfolios. Include the architecture diagram, a sample trace showing cost/latency per run, and the one-command containerized run. On your resume: 'Productionized an LLM agent with an eval harness (LLM-as-judge + regression), tracing, injection-defense guardrails, and cost/latency controls, served behind a containerized API.' Emphasize that it runs locally with your own API key and reproducibly in Docker, and frame it as the capstone that unifies the entire agent-engineering ladder.
